opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think literature search is one of the most underrated uses. Physics has an enormous literature, much of it decades old, written in different notations, sometimes in different languages, scattered across journals that nobody reads anymore. Very often you're working on a problem and you have a strong suspicion that someone, somewhere, has already computed some piece of it, maybe a particular integral, or a perturbation expansion around some black hole spacetime, but finding it with keyword search is nearly impossible because you don't know what they called it.

What these models can do is understand the *content* of what you're looking for. You can describe the calculation in your own words, in your own conventions, and it can say, "This looks like what so-and-so did in a 1970s paper on the Kerr geometry, though they used a different coordinate system." That's something that used to require either a lot of luck or knowing the right senior person to ask. It can save weeks.

And there's a second benefit that I think matters even more: it helps you avoid reinventing the wheel, and it helps you give proper credit. In science, connecting your work to what came before isn't just courtesy, it's how the field builds on itself. If a tool can surface the forgotten paper that already had half the answer, everyone benefits, including the person who wrote it fifty years ago.

Of course, you still have to check. You go read the paper, you verify the result. But as a way of pointing you to the right place in a vast library, it's become genuinely transformative for how I work.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can match a calculation in the scientist’s current work to prior research, including forgotten papers, helping connect new work to what came before.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the literature search piece is the one where I've seen the most immediate, concrete payoff. I work on black hole physics, on the theory side, and the thing people outside the field don't appreciate is how much of your week can disappear into just figuring out whether something has already been done. You have an idea, you think it's new, and then you spend two days digging through arXiv trying to find the one paper from 1998 that already worked it out in a slightly different notation.

What the AI tools are good at is exactly that kind of problem. I can describe the calculation I'm thinking about in my own words, in physics language rather than keywords, and it will come back with "this looks like what so-and-so did in the context of Kerr perturbations" or "there's a related result in the gravitational lensing literature you might not have looked at." That cross-pollination is really valuable, because the fields are siloed. Someone in numerical relativity might have solved a problem that someone in the analytic community doesn't know about, just because they use different vocabulary.

Now, I want to be careful here. It makes things up. It will confidently cite a paper that doesn't exist, or attribute a result to the wrong person. So I treat it the way I'd treat a very well-read but slightly unreliable colleague. It gives me a starting point, and then I go verify. But even with that caveat, the starting point is often much better than what I'd get from a keyword search, and it saves me from the worst failure mode, which is spending months on something that was done thirty years ago.

The other thing I'd say is that it lowers the barrier to entering an adjacent field. If I want to understand what the observational people at the Event Horizon Telescope are actually worried about, I can get a reasonable map of that literature in an afternoon instead of a semester. For a theorist, that's a real change in how you can work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI can match a calculation they are considering to related results in other research areas, helping uncover connections across fields with different terminology.

astra-6.text:
One of the hardest parts of research is knowing whether somebody has already answered the question you’re thinking about. The literature is enormous, and the relevant result might be in a different field, expressed in language you wouldn’t think to search for. AI could be very useful for making those connections.

What I’d want is a tool that helps me find the papers, understand why they might be relevant, and then go back to the original sources and check. That could save a tremendous amount of time, but it could also lead to new ideas—because sometimes the thing you need is a connection to work you didn’t know existed.

r001.rationale: The response describes connecting a research question to relevant work in other fields, but does not clearly identify connections to new developments in the scientist’s own work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest value is helping you find connections you might otherwise miss. When you enter a new area, you don’t necessarily know the terminology, who has worked on a problem, or whether the same idea appears under a different name. Being able to describe what you’re looking for in ordinary language and get pointed toward relevant papers could be enormously useful.

But you still have to read those papers and check that they actually support what the AI says. I’d want it to help me navigate the literature, with clear sources, rather than replace the work of understanding it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can reveal connections and help find related papers, but it does not connect new developments in a scientist’s own work to other research.
